questions.q: What is the primary difference in purpose between README.md and RUNBOOK.md in this project?
options: They are redundant — either file alone would be sufficient
README.md explains what the project is and how to run it; RUNBOOK.md explains how to operate and troubleshoot it once running
RUNBOOK.md is for end users; README.md is only for internal engineers
README.md contains the Helm chart source code; RUNBOOK.md contains the Kubernetes manifests
questions.explain: README.md orients a reader to what the project is, its architecture, and how to run it. RUNBOOK.md is a separate, operational document focused on diagnosing and responding to real failure scenarios once the system is running.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what do interviewers care about most regarding a project like this?
options: The raw volume of YAML written
The specific decisions made and the reasoning behind them, not just the fact that the infrastructure exists
Whether the project uses the newest possible Kubernetes API version
Whether every single Kubernetes feature from the course was used somewhere
questions.explain: The lesson frames a strong interview answer around decisions — why an HPA went on checkout and not product-catalog, why Helm was chosen, why Secrets were handled a certain way — rather than simply describing what was built.

questions.q: When asked 'What would you add if this ran for real?', which answer best reflects the approach this lesson recommends?
options: Claiming the project is already complete and nothing more is needed
Naming specific, reasonable next steps left out of the capstone's scope, such as a live GitOps controller and a PodDisruptionBudget, and explaining why they were out of scope
Avoiding the question since the capstone was explicitly scoped
Saying you would rewrite the entire project in a different tool
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly recommends naming concrete next steps (a live GitOps controller, a PodDisruptionBudget) and explaining the scoping decision — this demonstrates judgment rather than treating the capstone's boundaries as a weakness to hide.

questions.q: What is a PodDisruptionBudget, as introduced in this lesson's context?
options: A Helm values file controlling resource requests and limits
A resource that limits how many Pods of a workload can be voluntarily disrupted at once, such as during a node drain
A budget tracking the dollar cost of running a Deployment
A field inside an Argo CD Application manifest controlling sync frequency
questions.explain: A PodDisruptionBudget protects availability during voluntary disruptions (like kubectl drain for node maintenance) by capping how many Pods of a workload can be taken down simultaneously — named here as a reasonable next step beyond the capstone's scope.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend practicing a roughly thirty-second answer for describing the capstone, rather than a longer walkthrough?
options: Because interviewers are not allowed to ask follow-up questions
Because a concise, decision-focused summary is more effective in an interview setting than reciting implementation details at length, and follow-ups are where depth gets demonstrated
Because the project is too simple to describe in more than thirty seconds
Because interview time limits are always exactly thirty seconds per question
questions.explain: A tight, decision-focused summary communicates the project's substance quickly and invites the natural follow-up questions where deeper technical detail and reasoning can be demonstrated — a long unprompted walkthrough tends to bury the key decisions.
